name: Mangaleswarar Temple, Sirukudi
deity: Shiva as Mangaleswarar (Sookshmapureeswarar), with the goddess Mangala Nayaki
tradition: Shaiva — a Paadal Petra Sthalam, sung by Sambandar
summary: Sirukudi, a short way west of Tirupampuram, honours Shiva as Mangaleswarar — also called Sookshmapureeswarar — with the goddess Mangala Nayaki. A Paadal Petra Sthalam sung by Sambandar, it keeps a tender tale: after Parvati won a game of dice on Mount Kailasa and Shiva withdrew from her sight, she made a lingam of a handful of sand and worshipped it here, and the lord, pleased, appeared and took her back. From that handful of sand, Sirupidi, the village takes its name.

sections.history: Sirukudi is an ancient Shaiva village near Tirupampuram, hymned in the seventh-century Tevaram by Sambandar and counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams. The stone temple is of the Chola period with later additions. Its layered names — Mangaleswarar for the goddess Mangala Nayaki, and Sookshmapureeswarar from the sthala legend — carry a tradition in which the lord, having grown 'subtle' and vanished on Kailasa, re-manifested here before his consort.
sections.architecture: The temple follows the Dravidian plan with a gopuram, prakara and the sanctum of Mangaleswarar; the goddess Mangala Nayaki has her own shrine. A modest delta temple, it keeps the quiet, intimate scale of the lesser-known Paadal Petra shrines. Its nearness to Tirupampuram, three kilometres to the east, makes it a natural companion visit for pilgrims in that part of the delta.
sections.legends: The sthala-purana tells that on Mount Kailasa, Parvati won a game of dice against Shiva, after which the lord withdrew and became subtle, vanishing from her sight. Grieving, Parvati came to this place and made a lingam of a handful of sand — sirupidi — and worshipped it with deep devotion. Pleased, Shiva appeared before her and accepted her once more. Because the lord, having grown subtle (sookshma) on Kailasa, re-manifested here, the place is called Sookshmapuri and the deity Sookshmapureeswarar; and from the handful of sand the village takes the name Sirukudi.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps the Shaiva festival calendar — Maha Shivaratri, Pradosham and the Margazhi season — at the quiet scale of a village shrine. The reunion legend gives the temple a gentle association with marital harmony and reconciliation, and local observances mark the Tamil months.
sections.experience: Sirukudi offers the pilgrim a tender story of separation and reunion at the heart of its worship — a goddess who won a game and then won her lord back with a handful of sand. The darshan of Mangaleswarar, close to the serpent-temple of Tirupampuram, rewards those who seek out the quieter Paadal Petra shrines with a story of love restored.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to midday and again from late afternoon into the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed in the outer corridors but not inside the sanctum; ask temple staff before photographing rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Sirukudi is in Tiruvarur district, about 3 km west of Tirupampuram and near Kuthalam; the nearest rail heads are Kuthalam and Mayiladuthurai, with local buses and taxis to the village.
